label: Salary / wages not paid by employer

entries.title: Deadline to pay salary
entries.summary: For monthly-paid employees, salary must be paid before the 7th day of the next month (earlier deadlines apply for daily/weekly wages). If you resign, are removed, dismissed or retrenched, or the establishment closes, your pending wages must be paid within 2 working days.
entries.use_when: Any unpaid salary case; full-and-final dues after leaving.
entries.caveat: The Code took effect on 21 Nov 2025 but some central/state rules are still being notified, so enforcement details may differ by state. Whether the 2 days count from resignation or last working day is debated.
entries.verified_via: LiveLaw / People Matters commentary on Section 17 (checked 2026-11-08)

entries.title: Wage claim before the labour authority
entries.summary: You can file a claim for unpaid wages before an authority appointed by the government (an officer of at least Gazetted rank, usually in the Labour Department). The claim should be filed within 3 years of the wages falling due; the authority tries to decide within 3 months.
entries.caveat: Which office handles it depends on your state and the type of establishment. Ask the local Labour Commissioner's office.

entries.title: Salary is a contractual promise
entries.summary: Your offer/appointment letter is a contract. Not paying agreed salary is a breach, and you can claim the dues through a civil recovery case if the labour route does not apply to you.
entries.use_when: Senior/managerial staff, or as a general legal basis.

entries.title: Practical order of steps
entries.summary: 1) Send a written demand by email and registered post. 2) If unpaid, approach the Labour Commissioner/labour office of your area with your proof. 3) Free legal aid (NALSA 15100) can help with the claim or a civil case.

entries.title: Free legal aid
entries.summary: Industrial workers and people below the income limit can get a free lawyer from the District Legal Services Authority. Call NALSA helpline 15100.

proof_checklist: Offer/appointment letter or any document showing salary
Past salary slips and bank statements showing earlier salary credits
Attendance records, emails or work you did in the unpaid period
Resignation/termination letter and relieving date (if you left)
Messages where the employer admits or promises to pay
lawyer_triggers: Employer has accused you of theft/misconduct or filed a police complaint
A salary cheque bounced (separate cheque bounce law, strict 30-day notice deadline)
Company is shutting down or insolvent
